# Track Zoom and Bypass EQ Troubleshooting Tree

The track title area's anomaly was initially described as “the zoom value does not roll back.” On review, that description is too broad. There are at least two situations in the field: in one, after the title area grows, it appears no longer to be constrained by the available area of the current window; in the other, a height relationship that was previously fine only appears wrong after the window size changes. The two symptoms look similar, but the recovery actions differ, so separate them by trigger order first.

The entry point still starts at `OpenUtau/ViewModels/TracksViewModel.cs`. From there, check downward from the track view state; do not infer from the path itself that all height calculations happen in the same place. For each reproduction, retain only the conditions that can change the assessment: whether the window was just resized, whether the current track count changed, whether the anomaly occurred after zooming in or out, and whether the title and content areas changed together. The track name, audio content, and listening result are not the primary records for this branch; do not mix them in yet.

```text
Title area vertical zoom anomaly
│
├─ Appears on the first zoom-in
│  ├─ Height changes with the window size
│  │  └─ First check the display relationship involving the available area
│  └─ Height does not change with the window size
│     └─ Retain the current height and zoom direction
│
├─ Appears only after consecutive zoom-ins
│  ├─ Recovers after zooming out
│  │  └─ Record the last direction change before the anomaly appeared
│  └─ Does not recover after zooming out
│     └─ Compare whether the title and content areas are still out of sync
│
└─ Becomes visible only after switching tracks
   └─ Retain the states before and after the switch; do not treat it as an upper-limit conclusion
```

If the title and content areas expand or shrink together, enter the overall view-size branch first. When the window has just been resized, a docked area has just changed, or the number of visible tracks has just changed, the apparent title-height difference may come from the redistribution of the entire view. First restore the window to a state close to the one before the anomaly, then perform one zoom operation. If the proportions recover together, record it as related to the overall view state. If the content-area proportion is normal but the title area remains abnormal, switch to the title-area-only branch.

Older records directly interpreted “the blank space remains after zooming out” as meaning that the height value had not rolled back. Retain only the symptom now: after zooming out, the display did not stay in sync with expectations. This may be related to the available area, the title-area calculation, or redraw timing; the blank space alone cannot establish that any particular value failed to update. In particular, when the window has also changed, do not treat one failed rollback as evidence that a fixed upper limit has failed.

When only the title area changes, distinguish where the anomaly appears. Exceeding expectations on the first zoom-in is not the same record as appearing only after consecutive zoom-ins. For the former, retain the current window state; for the latter, retain the last zoom direction before the anomaly appeared. If zooming in is normal and the anomaly appears only after changing the window, record the window change as the trigger. If a height difference or blank space remains after zooming out, record whether the title and content areas became unsynchronized after the rollback. A case that becomes visible only after switching tracks must also be listed separately; the switch may only make an existing state visible and does not mean the switch caused the anomaly.

The first round tried only refreshing the view. Sometimes that made the blank space disappear, so it was temporarily treated as recovered. Treat it as an observation action instead: if the symptom disappears after a refresh, the display state can be rebuilt; if it remains, the current display was not simply masked by a refresh. Neither result shows that the upper-limit determination is correct, and neither can replace recording the zoom direction and window conditions. If further investigation is needed, start from the state before the refresh rather than reasoning backward from the refreshed display.

The equalization issue has also been split up. “No effect” includes at least four situations: processing is already bypassed; the configuration does not stably enter the processing object; processing runs, but the input segment is not suitable for distinguishing it by listening; or the result is overwritten by another stage afterward. The first three can be checked near the current object. The fourth cannot be concluded from this record alone, so do not write it as the default explanation.

Before starting the equalization investigation, fix the same track, the same input segment, and the same configuration. For every comparison, confirm that the before and after results come from the same buffer range. If one side comes from the result of playing the entire passage and the other from a local segment, even an identical listening result cannot support a conclusion of bypass, configuration failure, or skipped processing. Align the comparison objects first, then discuss the result.

```text
Equalized output is identical or similar to the original input
├─ Current bypass state is clear
│  ├─ Bypassed
│  │  └─ Record unchanged samples as the expected path first
│  └─ Not bypassed
│     ├─ Configuration cannot be reproduced reliably
│     │  └─ Fix the configuration source and input, then compare again
│     ├─ Before and after are not from the same buffer range
│     │  └─ Invalidate the old comparison and retake the same range
│     ├─ Samples are exactly identical
│     │  └─ Check whether processing entered the target range
│     └─ Samples differ but sound similar
│        └─ Record a processing difference; do not label it bypassed
└─ Current bypass state is unclear
   └─ Stop at the configuration object; do not guess the state from listening
```

The correction that must be retained here is: an equalization result close to the original sound does not mean bypass. Bypass is an explicit processing state; a result close to the original may come from the input, parameters, comparison method, or listening conditions. Conversely, identical samples before and after processing cannot automatically show that the configuration is ineffective, because bypass should leave the samples unchanged. The troubleshooting table should record the state, whether the configuration is reproducible, the comparison range, and the result separately; none of these should replace another.

If the bypass state is already clear and bypass is the expected behavior, identical output can end this round of audio-result checks; there is no need to add more listening attempts. If processing is expected but the state remains bypassed, retain the configuration object and current state, then check whether the configuration actually entered the processing object. Do not change the input segment to hide a state mismatch; changing the segment can only change the listening result and cannot explain why the current state did not change.

If the system is not bypassed, first separate “samples are exactly identical” from “the listening result is similar.” Exactly identical samples are a technical symptom that can be investigated further; check whether the comparison range is the actual processing range. Similar listening is only an observation. If the samples already differ, it should not be categorized as bypass. Mixing the two forces later investigators to infer the state from a subjective description.

The two lines still share only the release window; they do not share a processing chain. The title-area branch produces height, available-area, and zoom-direction records. The equalization branch produces the bypass state, whether the configuration can be reproduced, and the before/after results from the same buffer. If both sides show anomalies in the same round, complete each side's minimal record separately first, then compare the order in which they occurred. Still unconfirmed: whether the title area's final upper limit is determined entirely by the available view area; and which inputs produce sufficiently obvious sample changes after equalization with a valid configuration.

# Track Scaling and Bypassed Equalizer Troubleshooting Tree

This troubleshooting record retains two phenomena that are often reported during the same stability check: the track header area appears too tall after vertical scaling, and the track equalizer sounds unchanged in some reproductions. Both occur within the current release window, but they have different entry points. For the former, start by checking the view area, header area, and scaling direction; for the latter, start by checking the effect state, configuration, and buffer. Do not assume that a refresh, a track switch, or an audition is a shared recovery action just because both issues are visible at the same time.

The header-area investigation starts at `OpenUtau/ViewModels/TracksViewModel.cs`. This is near the track view state and is suitable for first confirming the relationship between the post-scaling height and the available view area. For the equalizer, start with the current track's effect state and the results before and after processing. Similar file paths, UI locations, and occurrence times are not enough to show that the two issues share the same root cause.

First obtain evidence that can be compared. For the header area, retain only the relative heights of the header area and content area before and after scaling, the scaling direction, whether the window was just adjusted, and whether the issue appeared only after switching tracks. For the equalizer, retain only the same track, the same input segment, the current configuration, the bypass state, and whether the same buffer interval was compared before and after. If both occur, record the actual order: whether the display issue was seen first or the audio issue was heard first; do not use the result of one issue to fill in the missing information for the other.

If it is not possible to determine whether the header-area issue appeared after zooming in, zooming out, changing the window, or switching tracks, stop at the scaling branch first. If the equalizer comparison did not use the same input segment and the same buffer interval, stop at the effect branch first. Vague statements such as “it looks wrong” or “it sounds no different” can begin a bug report, but cannot support the technical judgments that follow.

```text
Investigation entry
├─ Track header area height appears abnormal first
│  ├─ Content area also becomes taller or shorter
│  │  └─ Enter the overall view size branch
│  └─ Content area does not change by a similar proportion
│     └─ Enter the header-area scaling limit branch
├─ No obvious equalizer change is heard first
│  ├─ Current bypass state is visible
│  │  └─ Enter the effect state branch
│  └─ Current bypass state is unclear
│     └─ Return to the configuration object; do not evaluate the output yet
└─ Both occur at the same time
   ├─ Each can be reproduced independently
   │  └─ Record them separately, then compare the trigger order
   └─ One of them cannot be reproduced
      └─ Do not use the result of the other to fill in the cause
```

## Header area: first determine which boundary was lost

“Header area too tall” is not a sufficiently specific result. The first step is not to continuously scroll to zoom, but to check whether the track content area also changes by a similar proportion. When the header area and content area change together, first suspect that the overall visible area was reallocated; only when the header area changes by itself should you enter the vertical scaling limit branch. Putting this step first helps prevent an apparent issue caused by a window change from being misrecorded as a height issue belonging to the header area itself.

### When the content area changes along with it

If the window was just resized, the docked area just changed, or the number of visible tracks just changed, the header area may appear abnormally tall simply because the entire view size was reallocated. In this case, first restore a window state close to the one before the issue, then perform scaling only once. Do not move the window, change the scaling direction, and switch tracks at the same time; even if the display recovers, you will not know which action changed the display relationship.

If the title area and content area return to their previous proportions together after the window is restored, record it as “related to overall view dimensions.” This does not mean the scaling branch has been ruled out; it means that the current instance first depends on the overall region. If the content area proportions are normal after the window is restored but the title area is still clearly too tall, switch to the title-area-only branch. What must be preserved here is the relative relationship before and after; there is no need to add unrelated audio content, playback position, or equalizer settings for troubleshooting.

Older records directly described “the blank space remains after shrinking” as the height value not rolling back. This wording has now been narrowed: the blank space remaining only shows that the current display is not synchronized with expectations. The window's usable area, the title-area calculation result, and the refresh timing may all be involved. Without preserving the window state, you cannot determine from the blank space alone which state failed to update.

When the overall-size branch is triggered, first check that these three records are complete: whether the window differed before and after the anomaly, whether the title area and content area changed together, and whether performing only one zoom operation can reproduce the proportional difference. If any item is missing, do not continue describing it as an “upper-limit failure.” The current task is to route the instance to the correct branch, not to attribute it to the implementation without sufficient state.

```text
The title area and content area change together
├─ The window state has just changed
│  ├─ The proportions recover together after restoring an approximately equivalent window
│  │  └─ Record it as related to overall view dimensions
│  └─ The title area remains abnormal on its own after restoration
│     └─ Switch to the title-area-only branch
├─ The window state has not changed
│  └─ Preserve the zoom direction and visible-area state
└─ It cannot be determined whether the window changed
   └─ Do not classify the instance as an upper-limit issue
```

### Only the title area changes

When only the title area has clearly increased and the content area has not changed in the same way, first record what type of operation preceded the anomaly: it appeared on the first zoom-in; it appeared only after repeated zooming in to a certain state; it was normal after zooming in but appeared only after adjusting the window; the abnormal height or blank space remained after zooming out; or it became visible only after switching tracks. These are not implementation conclusions; they ensure that the next review does not have to start by guessing from “intermittent.”

When it appears on the first zoom-in, the current window state and zoom direction are sufficient as the first piece of the instance record. When it appears only after repeated zooming in, the last direction change before the anomaly must be recorded; the number of repetitions and the direction are themselves part of the behavior and must not be reduced to “intermittent.” When zooming in is normal but the anomaly appears only after changing the window, preserve the window change as the trigger condition. When it remains abnormal after zooming out, preserve the relationship between the title area and content area after zooming back out. When it becomes visible only after switching tracks, preserve the states before and after the switch, but do not write the switch action as the cause of the anomaly.

The track view model uses `Bounds` to represent the usable view area and uses it to constrain track height after vertical scaling. When checking the title-area upper limit, first keep the usable area unchanged, then perform zoom-in and zoom-out separately. If the anomaly appears only after the usable area changes, keep it in that branch; do not rewrite the behavior as a fixed-height threshold issue. If the usable area remains unchanged but repeated zooming can still exceed expectations, record the zoom direction and display state immediately before the anomaly is reached, for subsequent investigation through the track view state.

This requirement also explains why the final anomalous frame alone is insufficient. The final frame can show that the title area currently looks too tall, but it cannot show whether the usable area changed earlier, nor whether the issue appeared on the first zoom-in or only after repeated zooming in. The troubleshooting record needs the minimal operation sequence, not a larger number of screenshots.

### Zooming out does not restore it immediately

If the title area still looks too tall after zooming out, do not immediately restart the interface or switch tracks repeatedly. First compare whether the content area also retains the same height difference. If the content area has the same difference, return to the overall view dimensions branch. Only if blank space remains in the title area alone should you check whether switching tracks changes the display state. A change after switching only indicates that the display state was rendered again; only if it remains unchanged after switching should you preserve the states before and after zooming and continue checking the title area height and available area.

```text
The issue remains after zooming out
├─ The content area also retains the same height difference
│  └─ Return to the overall view dimensions branch
├─ Blank space remains only in the title area
│  ├─ The state changes after switching tracks
│  │  └─ Record the display change; do not conclude from this that it is fixed
│  └─ The state remains unchanged after switching tracks
│     └─ Preserve the title area height, available area, and zoom direction
└─ It recovers only after zooming in once more
   └─ Mark it as direction-dependent; do not substitute the refresh result for reproduction
```

There was one observed case where the view appeared to recover after a refresh. Refreshing can be used as a temporary observation step, but not as a criterion for recovery. It may have recalculated the display state, or it may only have redrawn the current screen; this page does not combine these two possibilities into a single conclusion. When recording the result, simply write “the visible symptom disappeared after refreshing” or “the issue remained after refreshing”; do not write “refreshing fixed the upper limit.”

If it recovers only after zooming in once more, do not directly describe that result as the zoom upper limit having been corrected either. At minimum, it indicates that the displayed result depends on the direction of the operation, but it is still insufficient to determine at which step the height is evaluated. In cases like this, it is especially important to preserve the sequence of zooming out and then zooming in again, rather than keeping only the final screen showing recovery.

### Stop conditions for the zoom branch

Stop broadening the scope when any of the following occurs: both the title area and the content area change, but the window state was not preserved; only the final screenshot remains, with no zoom direction; the issue appears as the window changes, but there are no before-and-after states; zoom correctness is judged solely from the result after switching tracks; or a single reproduction changes the window, zoom direction, and track selection at the same time. Stopping does not mean closing the issue; it means the current record is insufficient to support a deeper assessment.

One point concerning the upper limit for vertical zoom in the track title area remains unconfirmed. It requires event records of inputs and outputs, rather than adding speculation about equalization, waveform rendering, or the track content area. UTA-208 can be used to navigate to this maintenance entry; the card already has records of reproduction and transfer from review, and the unconfirmed observed case should remain unconfirmed.

## Equalization: first confirm whether processing should occur now

First rephrase “equalization makes no audible difference” as a question that can be checked: is the current effect bypassed; if not, has it received a valid configuration and processed the buffer range being compared. Bypass is not a failure result. The bypass path is expected to leave samples unchanged, so identical results before and after processing cannot, on their own, prove that the configuration was not received, nor can they prove that the filter failed.

Before listening or comparing, keep the same track, the same input segment, the same configuration set, and the same buffer range fixed. If you change the playback position or segment each time, input differences will become mixed into the results; if the before-and-after data does not cover the same range, the results are not comparable, however similar the full segment sounds. First align what is being compared, then assess the state and output.

BiquadEQ reports via `IsBypassed` whether the current configuration bypasses processing and leaves the audio samples unchanged. Read this state first; do not infer it backward from what you hear. In scenarios where the input itself changes very little, the clip is too short, or the processing difference is difficult to hear, listening impressions are especially unsuitable for determining bypass.

```text
Equalizer output is identical or similar to the original input
├─ IsBypassed is true
│  ├─ Bypass is the current expectation
│  │  └─ Unchanged samples are the expected result; end output troubleshooting for this round
│  └─ Processing is the current expectation
│     └─ Recheck why the configuration is still keeping the effect processor bypassed
├─ IsBypassed is false
│  ├─ The configuration source is unknown or cannot be reproduced
│  │  └─ Fix the configuration and input first; do not evaluate the processing result
│  ├─ The before-and-after comparison is not from the same buffer range
│  │  └─ Discard the old comparison and retrieve the same range again
│  ├─ The samples are exactly identical
│  │  └─ Recheck whether processing reached the target range
│  └─ The samples differ but sound similar
│     └─ Record this as a processing difference, not as bypass
└─ IsBypassed cannot be obtained
   └─ Stop at state confirmation; do not use listening to fill in the conclusion
```

### Bypass is true

If `IsBypassed` is true, the first question is “Was this configuration supposed to bypass processing in the first place?”, not “Why couldn’t I hear any effect?” If bypass is the current expectation, unchanged samples are the expected result, and output troubleshooting for this round can stop here. If the operator clearly wants to use the equalizer but the current state remains bypassed, retain the configuration object and bypass state, and recheck whether the configuration actually entered the processing object. Do not switch to another piece of audio to conceal the state mismatch.

BiquadEQ applies filter parameters through `Configure` and processes audio after a valid configuration rather than remaining bypassed. If it is still bypassed after configuration, this page only requires recording the before-and-after states. This alone cannot directly establish that the parameters are corrupted, the filter has failed, or the audio chain was never called at all; those conclusions require different field evidence. Wording in old issue reports that describes “bypass” as “the processor is not working” can still help identify the symptom, but it is no longer used for determination. Bypass, whether configuration was attempted, whether the configuration is valid, and when processing begins are different questions.

A true bypass state does not require an immediate reset either. If the goal of the current reproduction is specifically to confirm the bypass path, resetting would discard the state that needs to be observed. Only when preparing to start a new round and after the current bypass state has been recorded should the reset be treated as a separator between two observations.

### Bypass is false, but the output still sounds like the original

When `IsBypassed` is false, first confirm that the configuration source can be reproduced consistently, then confirm that the before-and-after data comes from the same buffer range. When the configuration source is not fixed, alternating bypass states and listening impressions must not be written up as random; each occurrence may simply be using a different configuration. When the input or range is not fixed, a single matching sample result also cannot be attributed to the processing entry.

The distinction between “the samples are completely identical” and “the listening impression is similar” must be kept clear here. The former is a definite technical phenomenon: only when the configuration is reproducible, the state is not bypassed, and the comparison range is the same is it worth continuing to check whether processing has entered the target range. The latter is only an observation: if the samples already differ, even if the listening impression is similar, it should be recorded as a processing difference rather than reclassified as bypassed. This prevents the subjectivity of listening impressions from being mixed into the state determination.

After configuration, BiquadEQ processes audio in place within the specified buffer range via `Process`, while bypass leaves the samples unchanged. The key check is therefore whether the comparison range is the same as the processing target range. If only the result for the entire audio segment is available, but it is unknown which range was processed, first fill in the range information; do not skip this branch just because the entire playback sounds unchanged. When the data before and after processing comes from different buffer ranges, the previous comparison should be explicitly invalidated rather than continuing to add listening-test records based on it.

If the samples are completely identical, first check again whether processing entered the target buffer range. This does not amount to concluding that `Process` did not execute: under the currently observable conditions, it only puts the range relationship first again. If the samples differ but the listening impression is similar, retain the difference and the input conditions; there is no need to change the segment or broaden the scope of the issue just to obtain an obvious listening result.

### Handling repeated configuration changes

When the bypass state or listening impression alternates during repeated operations, record separately for each configuration whether the configuration, state, and input were consistent. As long as any one of these is not fixed, the result cannot be written up as unstable processing behavior. The most common mistake is to see that two listening tests differ and immediately attribute the difference to the effect processor; when the objects being compared have changed, there is insufficient basis for that attribution.

BiquadEQ’s `Reset` clears the filter’s runtime state, so subsequent configuration and processing start from a clean state. When the comparison needs to start over, treat it as a state action between the two observations: first complete the current record, reset, apply the same configuration, and finally compare only one fixed input segment. Resetting does not replace configuration checks, nor does it mean that the result before the reset was necessarily incorrect; it only prevents the previous run’s state from carrying over into the next round.

Stop the EQ branch in any of the following situations: it is unknown whether the current state is bypassed; the input segment or track was changed during the same round of comparison; the configuration object was not retained; only “cannot hear a difference” remains, with no sample or range information; the data before and after processing comes from different buffer ranges; or the result needs to be explained using the state of another effect processor that has not yet been confirmed. The stopping point is intended to let the next attempt continue from a clear state, not to turn an ambiguous listening description into a conclusion.

UTA-225 is used to navigate the stable reproduction issue for bypassable EQ. User paths not covered should still be written back to that card. The card can identify the entry point in the field; it does not replace the branch decisions here concerning bypass, configuration, and processing ranges.

## When the two lines can converge again

Only when the title area and EQ are each reproducible should you compare whether they share the same trigger timing. The fact that can be compared is narrower: whether the title-area anomaly always appears after a particular display-state change, and whether the EQ bypass state also changes in the same operation sequence. Even if the order is the same, record it first as a correlated observation rather than directly writing it up as a common root cause.

If the header-area issue is reproducible, while the equalization issue can only be described by how it sounds, complete the header-area record first. Conversely, if the equalization bypass state and processing range can be held fixed, while the header area only occasionally looks too tall, complete the equalization record first. Each investigation has its own stopping criteria; they do not need to be wrapped up in the same round. Forcing the two into a single fault would make even the usable partial states meaningless.

For the current follow-up check, start the header-area investigation from the track-view state in `OpenUtau/ViewModels/TracksViewModel.cs`, and verify the relationship between the available view area and the height after vertical zooming; for equalization, first obtain `IsBypassed`, then verify the state after `Configure` and the buffer range compared by `Process`. DOC-22 cover compatibility checks for curve-paste clamping, undo, and the DiffSinger variance patch. Only turn to those checks once the equalization results have ruled out bypass and processing-range issues, and the situation actually involves that set of objects; do not treat them as the default next step for abnormal track header-area height.

Additional stopping criteria: if reproduction results for the same track differ before and after bypass, retain the input buffer, zoom value, and effect instance identity; until all three are aligned, do not attribute waveform differences to equalization parameters or expand the investigation to adjacent tracks.

# Curve Undo and Variance Patch Compatibility Workflow

This verification has two tracks. Do not treat curve editing and the DiffSinger variance patch as a single call chain.

For curves, move away from the old investigation entry point first. Previously, an issue name or call name would usually lead to `OpenUtau.Core/Ustx/UCurve.cs`, followed by a search for declarations near `ucurve` and `uexpressiondescriptor`. Compatibility should now be checked through repository regression tests: paste a segment of an expression curve directly, check the user-visible result after clamping, then undo and confirm that the curve returns to its state before the paste. Regression assertions should check results, not whether a particular internal helper function was called. With this change, files remain entry points for investigation, while regression tests become the basis for judging compatibility.

Procedure:

1. First save a copy of the curve's state before the paste, and record the paste region and out-of-range points; do not modify the original sample first.
2. Paste within the same editing session, inspect the clamped curve, and confirm that out-of-range values do not carry through to the displayed result.
3. Undo immediately afterward, and compare the curve, selection, and subsequent editing state. Any clamped result remaining after undo counts as a failure of this regression test.
4. Record the failure symptoms together with the regression entry point, then return to `UCurve.cs` to inspect nearby declarations; do not settle implementation ownership prematurely just because the entry-point filename is the same.

For the variance patch, move from the usage described on the help page to verification in an actual directory. First use the existing help page to find the call entry point, then run it once in a directory with no preset state. The check here is whether the cache can handle the rendering state after the patch is merged; do not substitute the clamped curve-paste result for this check. Leave the directory as it is for the first run, and only rerun with the same input on the second run, to distinguish “creating the cache for the first time” from “reading an existing cache.” If the call cannot complete in an empty directory, record the step where it stops and return to the help-page entry point. Do not keep guessing about the variance patch implementation based on UCurve.cs.

Keep the old paths for both migrations: while the new regression tests or empty-directory checks are not yet stable, issue names, call names, and `OpenUtau.Core/Ustx/UCurve.cs` can still be used for manual tracing. But the old paths only help locate things; they cannot replace checks of user-visible results or cache behavior.

# Package Version and Phoneme Timing Proposal

This round puts package version selection and clearing phoneme timing overrides in one proposal, but they are separate implementation tracks. The former handles multiple version strings in the registry; the latter handles whether the original state can be restored after an edit clears the overrides.

There are two tentative directions for package versions: continue comparing strings in text order and add exceptions for special formats as they come up; or first extract comparable semantic components, then select the higher version from the valid candidates. The former requires fewer changes; the latter keeps the rules more centralized. Handling of invalid strings, missing strings, and equal versions is still undecided.

Clearing phoneme timing overrides cannot mean “set to zero.” Before execution, save whether each override exists and its value. During execution, clear the attack and release overrides; on undo, write back the original state. No override and a zero-valued override are not the same input.

The first draft framed both issues as one interface change. After review, they were split into two proposal tracks. Package versions concern a candidate set; clearing phoneme overrides concerns object state before and after a command. They can be reviewed together, but cannot share inputs, failure symptoms, or rollback actions.

For package versions, both text sorting and parsed sorting remain options. Text sorting leaves the read path almost untouched, but version component counts, prerelease markers, and missing fields will keep requiring extra checks. Parsed sorting first takes the version strings from registry entries, extracts comparable semantic components, and then selects a result from the candidates that parse successfully.

A parse failure cannot simply be treated as the lowest version. An invalid string should not displace a valid candidate because its raw characters sort higher. Missing strings cannot automatically be grouped with malformed strings either: one means no value was provided, and the other means an unreadable value was provided. An empty registry and a registry where every entry is unusable also need to be observed separately. For equal valid versions, do not add sorting by name or input position yet, unless an existing stable order can be confirmed from the existing path.

Experiments cannot retain only the final version. Keep the original candidates and their order, the candidates that actually participated in comparison, and the final candidate or empty result. This is needed to distinguish whether a result changed because of parsing, filtering, or tie handling. During migration, retain the registry's original strings; do not change the values first to hide differences between the old and new behavior.

The phoneme track is narrowed to an undoable command. Before execution, save each override's presence and value. During execution, clear the attack and release overrides; on undo, restore the snapshot. Fields that originally had no override cannot be represented by zero, or undo will create a new zero-valued override.

Redo needs its own investigation. After the first clear, the object no longer carries the original overrides; rereading the object during redo would only return the cleared state. Whether the command or the undo group state should hold the snapshot is still undecided. The sequence of clear, undo, and redo must be exercised.

Record timing experiments for four classes of objects: attack override only, release override only, both present, and neither present. For each class, save the presence and value before execution, after clearing, and after undo, and check that the command has not also recalculated neighboring phonemes.

The two tracks have separate rollback conditions: if version sorting produces an unexplained change in valid candidate order, retain the original input and roll back the change; if phoneme undo loses an original override or writes a zero-valued override to an object with no override, stop integrating it into the editing path. `OpenUtau.Core/Format/Wave.cs` is still only a starting point for tracing back; the actual references for the package registry and editing commands must be confirmed individually.

versions.body:
# Package Version and Phoneme Timing Plan

The earliest record began with a path related to `wave`. At the time, files near the entry point were treated as the implementation locations for both issues, and package version selection and phoneme coverage restoration were written up as a single API adjustment. After review, both judgments were withdrawn. `OpenUtau.Core/Format/Wave.cs` can still serve as a starting point for tracing back, but it no longer determines implementation ownership; registry reads and references to editing commands must be checked separately going forward.

There was also an early misreading of the clearing direction: once an action enters the undo group, restoration will happen automatically. The counterexample is that an undo group can delimit a single edit action, but it cannot save the envelope coverage from before execution on behalf of the command. Once the fields are cleared during execution, reading them from the current object during undo finds that the original state no longer exists. The two directions remain in the same proposal because they share a review window, not because they share a state model.

For package versions, first try semantic comparison after parsing instead of continuing to pile exceptions onto text sorting. Version text in the registry is first parsed into comparable components, and selection takes place among the available candidates. This direction does not attempt to define all historical spellings at once; it only separates character order from version order. If changes in version-part length, pre-release markers, and missing fields continue to be handled by text rules, each new spelling may require maintainers to add another special case; the parsing path at least concentrates the differences at a single selection entry point.

One boundary must be retained here: an entry that fails to parse cannot participate in a highest-version selection that claims to be valid, but the presentation of the failure has not yet been decided. The entry can be skipped with a diagnostic left behind, or the caller can receive a distinguishable result; the current material is insufficient to merge the two directions. Missing version text likewise cannot simply be treated as a format error. The experiment output must preserve both original states instead of leaving only “no version.”

Text sorting will not be removed directly in this round. It is the comparison path for rollback; its advantage is that the read surface is small and the old candidate list can participate in comparison directly. The cost is that every new version spelling may require another explanation of why character ordering remains valid. The migration cost of parsed sorting is different: an old registry may produce a different candidate order under the new rules, and if callers depend on that order, the change must be visible in observation rather than comparing only the final returned text.

The package version experiment retains three layers of results:

1. The raw candidates received by the registry and their original ordering;
2. The successfully parsed candidates that actually participated in comparison and their ordering;
3. The final selected candidate, or an empty result when there is no selectable candidate.

The third layer alone is insufficient to explain a regression. The final value may have changed because the parsing rules differ, because a candidate was excluded, or because the handling of tied candidates changed. An empty registry, a set in which all candidates are unavailable, and a set containing both valid and invalid text must be recorded as different inputs; they cannot all be reduced to “no version.” If a candidate is missing text, record the absence; if text exists but cannot be parsed, record the original text and the failure state; the two samples must not be covered by the same empty value.

No new rule will be added for ties between identical valid versions for now. Without existing evidence, sorting by name or list position would create a secondary semantic that was not previously specified. If the existing read path has already left a stable order, it can be reused in the experiment results with the original input noted; if not, leave the tie as an unresolved item. Temporarily choosing a secondary key to obtain stable output would make rollback unable to determine whether a change came from the primary comparison or from the newly added tie rule.

The rollback conditions for the version direction are narrowed to two cases: an unexplained change in the order of valid candidates after parsing, or a previously usable candidate being excluded without the parsed result explaining why. If either occurs, retain the registry's original input and roll back the parsing changes. An empty result must not be packaged as a successful selection, nor may the original registry data be modified during migration to eliminate differences between old and new outputs. Whether the diagnostic should be directly visible to the caller Fang Ke is to be decided after the call relationships are confirmed.

On the phoneme timing side, the recommendation is to implement “clear coverage” as an undoable command and not recalculate phoneme timing values after clearing. Before command execution, obtain the target phoneme's envelope coverage state; during execution, clear attack- and release-related coverage; during undo, restore it from the snapshot. The saved content must include at least whether each coverage item exists and its corresponding value; saving only the values is insufficient to distinguish an absent state from zero-valued coverage.

This distinction affects the next edit. If a field that originally had no coverage is written as zero during undo, it becomes a new coverage. For input with only a release item, undo must not also create an attack item; the same applies when there is only an attack item. When both items exist, they must be restored separately; when neither exists, the state after undo must still have no coverage. The restored object is the same phoneme object from before execution; historical state must not be inferred from a same-named object in the current list.

Redo is an independent branch. The first execution has already cleared the coverage; if redo reads the snapshot from the object again, it will read the cleared result rather than the value from before the first execution. What remains undecided is whether the snapshot is held by the command instance or by the undo-group state. The two storage locations cannot be judged equivalent from a single execution; observe whether the snapshot still points to the original state across consecutive clear, undo, and redo operations. If the object is reacquired after undo, also confirm that the fields of the same editing object are restored rather than creating another coverage that merely looks identical.

The timing experiment records three moments for the same phoneme: before execution, after clearing, and after undo; then it adds the state after redo. The inputs must be divided into at least four categories: attack coverage present, release coverage present, both present, and neither present. For each category, verify whether the coverage is cleared, whether the presence state after undo returns to the original state, whether the values return to the original values, and whether redo produces the cleared state again. Testing only a single button click cannot cover these four categories; if the test entry point cannot construct one of them, retain the gap instead of substituting a default object.

Adjacent phonemes serve only as boundary observations. The clearing target is the current phoneme's timing coverage, not a recalculation of the entire adjacent chain and not a replacement of the fade-in and fade-out calculations. Confirm that after command execution and undo, adjacent objects still retain their original references and that the snapshot has not been written back to a later replacement with the same name. If the fading behavior of adjacent phonemes changes, record it separately rather than treating it as within the scope already covered by the clearing command.

The candidate comparisons retained for this round are as follows:

| Object | Candidate | Current trade-off |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Package version | Text sorting with exceptions | Smaller change, but exceptions will increase with new version spellings |
| Package version | Semantic comparison after parsing | Trial direction; invalid items and ordering differences need to be observed |
| Phoneme coverage | Record only the clearing action | Cannot restore original values or the no-coverage state |
| Phoneme coverage | Command saves a pre-execution snapshot | Trial direction; the snapshot's holding location still needs to be determined |

The two trials should not borrow each other's rollback mechanisms. Package version rollback depends on retaining the original candidates and the old selection result; reloading the project cannot replace that. Phoneme command rollback depends on the pre-undo snapshot; refreshing the project cannot replace that. Putting both into the same broad change would make it impossible to tell during a failure whether the result changed during candidate filtering, version comparison, field clearing, or restoration.

During migration, preserve the version text verbatim and record ordering differences verbatim as well. Initially limit the phoneme command to clearing the timing coverage itself; do not also fold in adjacent phonemes, track state, or package version refresh. Note addition and rollback for offset components, and identity routing for track-effect notifications, already have their own local records; this proposal does not combine them into the additional validation scope.

Five items still need confirmation: the complete range of syntax acceptable for version text; whether invalid items should be skipped and recorded or cause the caller to receive a diagnostic; whether identical valid versions already have an established secondary order; whether the snapshot is ultimately held by the command object or the undo-group state; and whether, when the phoneme envelope is missing, the clearing command should skip, report an error, or create an empty undo entry. Also confirm whether the test entry point can construct the four coverage states without modifying adjacent phonemes. Until confirmation, both lines are only trial proposals, not published API decisions.

versions.body:
# Offset Components and Effect Notification Troubleshooting Tree

Treat the symptoms as two cases: adding a note in a voice component with an offset, then seeing a result different from before the addition when rolling back; and, after changing a track effect, receiving the change on an object that does not appear to be the track just modified. They were once put on the same troubleshooting path because the earliest entry point was `OpenUtau.Core/Editing/NoteBatchEdits.cs`; new notes, component position, and note duration can all be examined from here.

The old record said, “Just follow the add command first.” That was still useful for the first symptom, but too broad for effect notifications. It is kept here to explain why the investigation initially went through the wrong entry point.

## Add Then Roll Back

First record the component offset, the note durations, and the note counts before and after the operation. The position shown in the piano roll cannot by itself be treated as the result; in an offset component, the displayed position and the position within the component may not be the same quantity.

- If the position has already deviated from expectations when the addition completes, stop at the add action and verify that the note entered the expected component. Do not use the later rollback result to explain the position yet.
- If the addition looks normal and the difference appears only after rollback, record separately whether the remaining residue is a note, duration, or position. The three types of residue correspond to different checkpoints and cannot be combined as “undo failed.”

Previously, a visible created note was treated as evidence that the rollback chain was working; that is no longer used. The creation result only shows that the add action reached a visible state and cannot replace the post-restoration check.

- If the two are the same, record whether the effect change occurred before or after the selection-state switch, then check for duplicate delivery. Duplicate notifications and an identity error are not the same thing.

# Decision on Separate Modifier-Key States for Notes

During the early investigation, additional visible changes persisted after note editing ended. These were tentatively attributed to incomplete cleanup of modifier-key transitions. At this stage, we will not create separate editing states for Ctrl, Alt, and key combinations; they are treated as conditions attached to the same editing gesture and cleared by a single exit handler when editing ends.

Two approaches were actually compared at the time. The first was to keep the combined check: remember the modifier conditions when editing starts, then discard them together when dragging, marquee selection, or pen-tool use ends. This keeps the state model small and lets the investigation work backward from the end action without first splitting out every key combination.

The other approach was to track modifier keys separately and handle key combinations as distinct input cases. This approach was not shown to be infeasible; there was simply no counterexample at the time showing that a modifier key could affect the result independently of the editing action. Splitting them out immediately would make mouse leave, tool switching, edit cancellation, and window focus loss all cleanup exits that needed checking, with no way during the investigation to tell which one was the source of the anomaly.

Decision: Keep the combined check for this round; do not add separate state transitions. Start the review with the state entry points near `OpenUtau/Views/NoteEditStates.cs` and check whether visible changes still remain after editing ends.

Open questions: When one key in a combination is released first, does it use the same exit handler as releasing all keys? Does canceling an edit also clear the same set of conditions?

# Decision on Independent Modifier-Key States in Note Editing

This record initially treated modifier keys in note editing as a temporary condition of an editing gesture. What was observed at the time was that, after an editing action was completed, the UI still showed changes that should not have remained, so the issue was attributed to an omission in exit handling. On that basis, the initial draft chose not to separate the states: capture a set of conditions when editing begins and clear them all when it ends; it did not require recording the press and release sequences for Ctrl, Alt, or key combinations step by step.

The old decision has not been deleted because subsequent investigations repeatedly looked for the cause in “end actions.” It explains why troubleshooting focused on what happened after dragging, marquee selection, and exiting the pen tool, and why the state model was not immediately expanded at the time. However, the initial draft directly turned an observed symptom into a judgment about state structure: something remaining after an operation ends does not mean that all modifier keys are merely one set of conditions that can be merged.

## Trade-offs in the Initial Draft

The first option on the table at the time was to treat modifier keys as supplementary information about whether editing was still in progress. This option had a clear assumption: regardless of which modifier keys the user used, once the same editing session ended, all related conditions should become invalid together. For troubleshooting the reported issue, this assumption had a practical benefit—only two things needed to be checked: whether editing had ended and whether any additional visible changes remained afterward.

The initial draft chose this option not because all input paths had been examined, but because the anomaly had only been reported after the action was completed. No continuous record was kept of pressing a key, establishing a combination, releasing one of the keys first, and releasing all keys. Without those segments, keeping the issue within end handling was a workable provisional judgment.

The other option was to separate individual keys and key combinations into independently observable local states. The initial draft set it aside mainly because of maintenance costs: once separated, the mouse leaving the editing area, canceling an edit, switching tools, and the window losing focus could all become distinct cleanup exit points. At the time, it was not yet possible to say whether these exit points would actually encounter different states, so they were not written up as new implementation requirements.

The phrase “keep the combined check; do not add independent state transitions” in the old document referred to this trade-off. It was a provisional conclusion intended to narrow the investigation at the time, not proof of how state should be stored. Later use of this sentence as evidence that “modifier keys should never have been separated” went beyond the material available to the initial draft.

## Counterexamples Found During Review

Returning to `OpenUtau/Views/NoteEditStates.cs` revealed a direct counterexample to the combined check. The local state was not a generic modifier-key flag; instead, there were three distinct names: `ctrlHeld`, `altHeld`, and `altShiftHeld`. They store the states of Ctrl, Alt, and Alt+Shift, respectively; at least within this object, individual-key and combination states were not collapsed into a single “modifier key present” boolean.

This changes the premise of the old decision; it does not fully explain the entire editing input system. The existence of separate fields shows that the earlier claim that “there is no need to store them independently” was too broad; however, the local state around this file alone still does not establish that every editing tool writes, reads, or clears these values in the same order. The previous record did not collect a complete call chain or retrace every mouse action individually.

In particular, `altShiftHeld` cannot be reconstructed from an abstract “a modifier key is currently active.” It preserves the combination relationship. If only a master switch is checked after editing ends, the sequence of holding Alt, then pressing Shift, and then releasing Shift first is collapsed into the same description of ended or not ended, leaving no way to determine when the combination state changed in the reported case.

`ctrlHeld` cannot be treated as an alias for Alt either. When early troubleshooting notes said “modifier key stuck,” they did not specify which local state was actually involved; such records could neither distinguish Ctrl from Alt nor reveal whether a key combination was involved. They could only show that the display after editing differed from expectations, not whether the lingering effect was in the input state, the tool result, or the handoff between the two.

## Correction to the Old Conclusion

“All modifier keys share one editing state” is no longer accepted as a description of the local state. When reviewing lingering effects in note editing, `ctrlHeld`, `altHeld`, and `altShiftHeld` should be examined separately, with the timing of their changes recorded. Whether editing has ended is still worth checking, but it can no longer be used as evidence that these states have been merged.

The scope of this correction is narrow. It applies only to the local note-editing state containing `NoteEditStates.cs`, preventing subsequent investigations from rewriting the existing distinctions as a check for any modifier key. It does not decide that all modifier keys should be permanently spread across more objects, nor does it require every read site to consider all three fields at once.

If a behavior depends only on Ctrl, first confirm that it observes `ctrlHeld`; if a behavior depends on the Alt+Shift combination, preserve the information represented by `altShiftHeld` rather than inferring the combination state from the fact that an edit has ended. Changes to Alt alone should be checked against `altHeld`. This decision concerns the granularity of records and judgments, not authorization for a complete rewrite of input logic.

The initial draft worried that separating the states would give each exit point its own reset logic. That concern has not been proven entirely wrong, but it is a maintenance concern rather than an observed behavioral fact. The available material does not answer whether end handling, cancellation handling, and focus-loss handling share a cleanup location; concern about having more exit points is not a reason to treat existing local fields as things that should not exist.

The old decision therefore retains its historical purpose: it records why end actions were checked first at the time and why the input state machine was not immediately explored in the investigation. However, the old decision is no longer a basis for adding editing logic. When this area needs to be changed, first list the fields being observed and their input, read, and clear locations, then discuss which exit points can be merged.

## Moments to Distinguish During Review

The early anomaly was described only as “there are still changes after editing,” which places the observation too late. Subsequent records should first state whether the symptom occurs when a modifier key is pressed, a combination is established, one key is released, editing ends, or editing is canceled. Only by recording the timing can we know whether to look back at local state or at the result produced by the tool.

Switching tools during editing is a branch for which no observations have yet been collected. There is currently no conclusion on whether the existing modifier-key state immediately affects the new tool. It cannot be assigned to end handling, nor can it be used to assert that switching tools resets any particular field; this branch needs to be recorded separately from a normal end action.

Canceling an edit must not be conflated with completing an edit either. The initial draft envisioned both as exit handling but did not observe whether they actually pass through the same cleanup location. If the anomaly occurs after cancellation, the record must at least preserve whether Ctrl, Alt, or Alt+Shift was involved at the time and whether the state had already changed before cancellation.

What happens when the window regains focus after losing it is likewise unconfirmed. The existing records contain no material supporting either possibility: that the combination state resynchronizes with the actual key state, or that it retains its previous value. No cleanup sequence is invented here; recording this as a branch to investigate is more useful than continuing to use the old assumption of unified exit handling.

The diagram below only shows which editing stages symptoms should be assigned to during investigation; it does not indicate that these stages already correspond to different implementation paths:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Editing
    state "Editing in progress" as Editing
    state "Editing finished" as Finished
    state "Editing canceled" as Cancelled
    state "Tool switch" as ToolChanged
    state "Window focus lost" as FocusLost
    Editing --> Finished : Finish editing
    Editing --> Cancelled : Cancel editing
    Editing --> ToolChanged : Switch tools
    Editing --> FocusLost : Lose focus
```

The four destinations in the diagram come from the exit points that the initial draft worried would broaden the investigation. They do not fill in the actual call relationships. At present, the only confirmed fact is that the local fields are already distinct; when each destination writes or clears the fields still needs to be investigated outward from the state file when the corresponding symptom occurs.

## The Retained Earlier Approach

“Look at end actions first” is not without value. If an anomaly occurs across multiple editing tools and only becomes apparent after actions are completed, end handling is still a reasonable starting point. The problem is that the old record mistakenly presented this starting point as a conclusion sufficient to rule out independent states, leading later investigators to look only for a unified reset without preserving the specific key sequence.

The additional visible changes mentioned in the early reports were not documented with reproducible visuals or input steps. That observation cannot distinguish lingering state from lingering tool results, nor can it show whether the issue occurs only in one particular tool. Because this original observation is itself incomplete, it can no longer be used to prove that Ctrl, Alt, and Alt+Shift should share the same state.

This record still contains the old judgment because it was once used as a starting point for release-period troubleshooting. Removing the initial draft would prevent those who later investigated end handling in the wrong direction from seeing the trade-offs made at the time. Preserving it while marking the premise overturned by the counterexample better serves the actual purpose of this material.

## Boundaries of the Current Decision

The current decision requires only this: when encountering a modifier-key anomaly in note editing, do not summarize every case as “modifier key stuck” anymore. Records should identify the stage at which it occurs and specify whether `ctrlHeld`, `altHeld`, or `altShiftHeld` is involved. Only then can individual keys, key combinations, and results remaining after editing ends be discussed separately.

The current decision does not require a new global state diagram for each field, nor does it claim that the three fields cover all input conditions. The local state in the file can serve as a starting point for investigation, but it cannot replace examination of a particular tool's input path. If the symptom appears in only one tool, first preserve the tool name and key sequence, then check its read sites near the state; only if multiple tools exhibit the same sequence is there reason to continue investigating shared end or reset handling.

Slicing transcription audio and multichannel trimming are outside the scope of this decision. That topic is retained separately in DOC-30; the correction to keyboard state on this page must not be extended into a judgment about audio interfaces.

The unconfirmed items remain: whether combination state is established by the order of key presses, supplied in advance by the input layer, or derived within editing state; whether the independent states are cleared in the same place or in different branches; and whether they resynchronize after focus loss. The old decision can no longer cover these questions, but the current review also lacks enough material to answer them.

# Proposal for Transcription Slicing and Multichannel Cropping

This page first captures the interface disagreement in the transcription-audio portion. The previous investigation found `OpenUtau.Core/Analysis/Some.cs` through `wave` and `audioslicer.slice`, but at the time that still wasn't enough to determine which layer was responsible for cropping, or which layer should convert multichannel audio to mono.

## The working hypothesis at the time

First have `audioslicer` perform `slice` based on the playback range, retain the returned `samples`, and then call `tomono` at analysis entry points that require mono. This way, frame calculation only deals with one well-defined sample buffer; if the channels are merged first, the cropping boundary may be reinterpreted by another layer.

Another option is to have the slicing API return a mono result directly. Its API surface for callers is smaller, but it would hide multichannel selection in the analysis entry point, and if the original channels need to be retained later, the migration cost would be higher. The first option is preferred for now, but there is not yet enough runtime evidence to support it.

## Parts to fill in

- Clarify whether the boundary of `wave` is based on the original samples or converted using `frame`.
- Use a stereo sample to verify the length and ordering of `samples` after `slice`.
- Confirm whether `tomono` should be a fixed step before analysis or belong only to a particular caller.

Keep `OpenUtau.Core/Analysis/Some.cs` as the verification entry point for now. TODO: record the inputs and outputs from one actual transcription and one multichannel crop.

# Proposal for Transcription Slicing and Multichannel Cropping

This proposal originated from an instance where “transcription runs, but the audio boundaries after slicing are unclear.” During the investigation, the names `wave`, `audioslicer`, and `audioslicer.slice` came up first, so the old notes treated `OpenUtau.Core/Analysis/Some.cs` as the main entry point. It is indeed a suitable place to check back, but the path itself does not establish that slicing responsibility has moved here or that multichannel conversion happens here. For now, we still examine direct adjacency in version `v_prev` of `internal/UTAU`, to avoid retroactively inserting call relationships organized later into the early proposal.

## Assessments Retained from the Old Draft

The early draft described the processing order as follows: first perform `slice` for the requested range, retain `samples` in the result, and then call `tomono` where analysis requires it. The reasoning at the time was straightforward: cropping should establish the time boundaries first, and channel merging should not change the interval to be extracted. The draft also retained an opposing view: if the slicing interface returned mono directly, callers would be simpler and test inputs would be easier to standardize.

These two statements cannot both be treated as the established interface. The first order is friendlier to callers that need to preserve multiple channels, but it requires downstream consumers to know that `samples` may still contain multiple channels; the second order reduces branching for consumers but may discard the original channel information at the entry point. The old draft did not provide enough samples to prove which cost had already been incurred, so “slice first, merge later” remains a candidate approach here, not a stable contract.

## Alternative Approaches

**A: Slicing returns the original channels, which are then merged at the analysis entry point.**

`audioslicer.slice` is responsible only for extracting samples within the requested range. `samples` in the return value retains the sliced result, and the channel count and layout are not silently changed at this layer. Before entering transcription analysis that requires mono input, call `tomono`. The benefit of this alternative is that responsibility boundaries are easy to describe: slicing handles only time, and merging handles only channels; the cost is that every analysis caller must explicitly determine whether it needs mono, rather than guessing from the return value's name.

**B: The slicing interface returns mono directly.**

`slice` performs cropping and `tomono` internally, and analysis callers consume only one type of buffer. This alternative suits local paths that have only mono analysis consumers, and the scope of changes appears smaller; however, if multichannel input is needed for other analysis or diagnostics in the future, the original samples will no longer be in the returned result. It also puts “correct cropping boundaries” and “correct channel downmixing” into a single interface call, making it difficult to distinguish which step caused a difference when a failure occurs.

**C: Provide both results.**

Retain the original slice and provide a separate mono buffer. This is the most complete approach, but it adds object fields and cache relationships; do not treat it as the default design before confirming that both types of consumers actually exist. If adopted, it must be clear whether the two results share boundaries and whether callers read `samples` or another derived value. Fields must not be added solely on the grounds of “compatibility.”

The current recommendation still leans toward A, but only for paths where callers can be confirmed to explicitly need `tomono` before analysis. If verification shows that all consumers require mono, B can be used as a local implementation; only if there are also consumers that preserve the original channels is there reason to continue evaluating C.

## What to Check During Reverification

First, keep the same segment of `wave` input fixed and change only the channel count. Use a mono sample to confirm the length and start and end positions of `slice`; use a two-channel sample to confirm whether callers can still recognize the layout of `samples`. “Same length” is not considered a sufficient result here, because two-channel data in interleaved and planar layouts may have the same total length but be read differently during `tomono`.

Next, keep the channel count fixed and change only the cropping range. Compare against the conversion results from `frame` and record whether the boundaries fall at the same sample positions; if the range comes from playback positions rather than original sample indices, identify the layer where conversion occurs. Finally, examine alternatives A and B separately: for A, confirm that merging happens before the analysis entry point; for B, confirm that the interface does not silently discard channel information still needed by other callers before returning.

These checks address only interface behavior, not the quality of the model's analysis itself. When transcription results improve or worsen, the change cannot be directly attributed to cropping order unless the boundaries, channel count, and `samples` for the same input have all been recorded. There is currently no run output available to cite. This gap must remain explicit; “slicing succeeded” cannot substitute for verification.

## Trade-offs Left by the Review

Before the review, the debate centered on “a simple interface” versus “preserving original data.” Putting `tomono` inside `slice` would shorten a single path, but the name would still make it look like a cropping-only interface, making it difficult for callers to realize that the data had already changed. Separating the two steps is more verbose, but it allows side-path reads that need the original multichannel data to remain available. If only the current transcription entry point is considered, B may require less code; if future audio diagnostics are also considered, A has a smaller rollback scope.

The follow-up card UTA-217 requested the missing run records for “transcription audio slicing and multichannel cropping.” By the later reverification, the relevant implementation had been completed on an existing branch, and the materials went straight into review; this shows that code changes were available to inspect, but does not by itself establish which of A, B, or C had been verified. Before review approval, the actual inputs and outputs should still be added to this page or the corresponding test records.

## Withdrawal Conditions and Unresolved Items

If the two-channel sample shows that A's `tomono` reads the wrong layout, withdraw the “slice first, merge later” order and pause at channel-layout verification, rather than reframing the issue as a boundary problem. If range conversion causes `frame` to produce different sample endpoints for the same request, withdraw the assumption that boundaries can be determined directly at the `slice` layer, and return to the conversion from playback positions to sample positions to check it. If B has already been adopted but some consumers still need the original channels, restore a readable original slice rather than making callers guess the channels again.

Still unresolved are the actual relationships in `OpenUtau.Core/Analysis/Some.cs` that connect `wave`, `audioslicer.slice`, and `samples`, and the exact call boundary of `tomono`. The starting point for verification is retained here; do not let the proposal's conclusions speak for the implementation prematurely.
